catalog_quote: Schebesta 1952: 393: "L'élision et la contraction des consonnes et des voyelles laissent des traces dans la hauteur du ton musical ... en efé, le pluriel se forme principalement avec le suffixe eni (ini) ... Lorsque ce -eni se fond avec la voyelle de la syllabe finale, par chute de la nasale, le pluriel est marqué par le ton haut." | Schebesta 1952 tone key (pp. 376-377): "Signes diacritiques: Ton musical: ' au-dessus de la voyelle ó: ton haut. - au-dessus de la voyelle ō, n'est jamais signe d'allongement, mais le signe du ton chanté, plus élevé que le ton parlé, ... ton haut ascendant (montant depuis le ton chanté). ... ton retombant (descendant depuis le ton chanté)." | Stuhlmann 1894: 460: "Alle Worte der Pygmäen bestehen aus einzelnen, abgerissen von einander ausgesprochenen Silben, die fast alle gleich stark betont werden." | Johnston 1902 II: 532-533: "They also have a peculiar singing intonation of the voice when speaking which is noteworthy. It consists usually in beginning the first syllable of a word on a low note, raising the voice on the penultimate syllable, and lowering it again on the last. It is almost a chant ... Their pronunciation is singularly staccato, every syllable being distinctly and separately uttered in a voice which is nearly always low and melodious."

It consists usually in beginning the first syllable of a word on a low note, raising the voice on the penultimate syllable, and lowering it again on the last. It is almost a chant ... [Ka lu ke ke]. Their pronunciation is singularly staccato, every syllable being distinctly and separately uttered in a voice which is nearly always low and melodious." | Stuhlmann 1894: 460: "Alle Worte der Pygmaen bestehen aus einzelnen, abgerissen von einander ausgesprochenen Silben, die fast alle gleich stark betont werden." | Schebesta 1952: 393: "...par chute de la nasale, le pluriel est marque par le ton haut."

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: All three quoted passages are present at the stated locators in the copies we hold under (1) Johnston 1902 vol. II pp. 532-533: djvu text lines ~17160-17185 read 'They also have a peculiar singing intonation of the voice when speaking which is noteworthy. It consists usually in beginning the first syllable of a word on a low note, raising the voice on the penultimate syllable, and lowering it again on the last. It is almost a chant, and expressed in musical notation would appear thus: [Ka lu ke ke] Their pronunciation is singularly staccato, every syllable being distinctly and separately uttered in a voice which is nearly always low and melodious' -- confirmed against the page scan printed…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is stated by any accessible source. The two first-hand early observers of Efe speech report (i) syllables uttered evenly, 'almost all equally stressed' (Stuhlmann 1894) and (ii) a word melody that starts low, peaks on the penultimate syllable and falls on the final (Johnston 1902, who also marks high/low pitch with acute/grave accents in his Bambute vocabulary). Schebesta 1952, from his own 1949-50 fieldwork, shows Efe pitch is lexically/grammatically functional (high tone marks plural, negation particles, contraction), i.e. Efe is a tone language; he offers no stress statement of his own. Net: tonal language; older impressionistic reports point to even syllable prominence with a penultimate pitch peak in citation forms, not to a contrastive or fixed dynamic stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Johnston: the low-penult-high-final-low melody holds 'usually'. Schebesta: high tone arises on final syllables from suffix fusion (-eni plural) and on negation particles.
new_statements.domain_note: Johnston's melody is described per word as spoken (isolated words elicited for vocabularies, effectively citation forms); Stuhlmann's remark is about words in his elicited list. Neither distinguishes word vs phrase level; both predate tonal analysis. Efe treated as a dialect of the Balese/Lese cluster by Vorbichler.
new_statements.identity_note: The first-hand prosodic remarks quoted are about the speech of Ituri Pygmies whom the authors did not call 'Efe': Johnston (1902) calls them 'Bambute' Dwarfs speaking 'a dialect of the Mbuba language' (upper Ituri / Fort Mbeni); Stuhlmann (1894) calls them 'Zwerge am Ituri' and notes their words agree with Wambuba (Mvuba) and Momfu (Mamvu). Schebesta (1952: 372-373) and the Africa 18 (1948: 54) note explicitly identify Johnston's 'Bambute' speech as Efe (efee1239) rendered with Efe phonetics, closer to southern Balese than to Mvuba. Modern descriptions treat Efe as a dialect within the Balese/Lese cluster (Vorbichler 1965, 1979, 1983: 'Balese-Obi, Balese-Dese-Karo, Mvuba, Mabendi, Mangbutu, Efe' as dialects of one group), so the authoritative phonology is a Lese (lese1243) grammar, Vorbichler 1965.

new_statements.quote: 2a. Tone Tone is both lexical and grammatical. In the MORU-MA'DI languages so far investigated (MORU, MA'DI, LOGO, LUGBARA) and in LENDU, three tone levels have been established, and the same would seem to be the case with MANGBUTU-EFE. ... Tone Classes in MANGBUTU-EFE have yet to be worked out ... In all languages there are Tone Classes in Nouns and Verbs. 2b. Stress Larochette reports a tendency towards stress on the penultimate syllable of a word or phrase in MANGBETU, accompanied sometimes by extra high tone as in neka- *kidri, headache. No such uniformity of stress pattern, however, has been found in the other Language Groups. Even such intimately closely allied languages as MORU and MA'DI have quite different stress behaviour.
new_statements.citation: Tucker, A. N. & M. A. Bryan. 1966. Linguistic Analyses: The Non-Bantu Languages of North-Eastern Africa. London: OUP for the International African Institute. (Moru-Mangbetu chapter: '2b. Stress' and MANGBUTU-EFE / LESE / MAMVU / EFE data.)

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record: classification tonal, empty rule (Schebesta 1952 tone marking / plural by high tone). Tucker & Bryan agree that the group is tonal (three levels 'would seem to be the case with MANGBUTU-EFE') and add no stress placement, so nothing changes; Johnston 1902's impressionistic penultimate rise (existing statement, read as unclear) is neither confirmed nor contradicted, and the chapter's penultimate statement belongs to Mangbetu, a different language.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Mangbutu-Efe group (Mamvu as exponent; Efe appears only in morphological data) the work says tone is lexical and grammatical with apparently three tone levels and tone classes not yet worked out; it gives NO stress placement for the group or for Efe, only the negative remark that no uniform stress pattern like Mangbetu's penultimate tendency has been found in the other language groups. The penultimate statement is about Mangbetu (after Larochette), the first-syllable rule about Moru and the final-vowel rule about Ma'di; none may be transferred to Efe.
new_statements.exceptions: none for Efe; the section's language-specific detail concerns Moru (initial stress even on a vowel prefix, vowel lengthening after a consonant, near-loss of some final syllables) and Ma'di (final-vowel stress), and phrase-level retention of word stress in both.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan treat the MANGBUTU-EFE group with MAMVU as main exponent; EFE (the Central Sudanic language of the Efe pygmies of the Ituri, closely allied to Lese/Balese) appears by name only in morphological data. Statements quoted are group-level (Mangbutu-Efe) or about other Moru-Mangbetu languages, not Efe-specific fieldwork.

sources.citation: Schebesta, Paul. 1952. Les Pygmees du Congo Belge. Trad. Henri Plard. (Mem. Institut Royal Colonial Belge, Sect. Sci. morales et politiques, in-8, T. XXVI, fasc. 2.) Bruxelles. Language chapter pp. 372-400; 'Phonetique efe et phonetique pygmeenne en general' pp. 391-393.
sources.note: No stress rule of his own. Quotes Stuhlmann (syllables 'presque toutes egalement accentuees') and Johnston (intonation low-penult high-final low, 'almost a chant', 'singularly staccato') as striking traits of pygmy phonetics (pp. 372-373). Own fieldwork (1949-50): Efe speech is 'hachee, saccadee' from pervasive glottal stops (p. 391); tone is functional: 'ton haut ascendant de la syllabe contractee' (p. 388 region), negation particles 'avec ton haut sur la syllabe finale' (p. 388), plural 'marque par le ton haut' when -eni fuses (p. 393), elision leaves traces 'dans la hauteur du ton musical'…
